tasks.label: Plan and build
tasks.description: Shape an idea, then turn it into working code.

tasks.label: Design interfaces
tasks.description: Visual direction, layout, components and interface quality.

tasks.label: Motion
tasks.description: Web and mobile animation, from first idea to review.

tasks.label: Review and test
tasks.description: Find defects, check flows in a browser and debug failures.

tasks.label: Security
tasks.description: Secure implementation, review and threat modeling.

tasks.label: Ship and deploy
tasks.description: Git, pull requests, releases and hosting.

tasks.label: Docs and files
tasks.description: Markdown, handoffs, office files, notebooks and Notion.

tasks.label: Images and media
tasks.description: Generated images, video, speech and transcription.

tasks.label: Working with agents
tasks.description: How agents load skills, split work and format answers.

startingPoints.task: Build a feature from a rough brief
Get a second opinion on my code
Design a screen that doesn’t look generic
Check a change in a real browser

yeknal-add-changelog.title: Changelog entries
yeknal-add-changelog.purpose: Adds or updates a Keep a Changelog entry based on the changes and history that can actually be verified, so release notes describe what shipped.
whenToUse: You are preparing a release and need the notes written up.
Work has shipped and the changelog has fallen behind.
You want entries grouped the Keep a Changelog way under Added, Changed and Fixed.

example.ask: Add a changelog entry for everything merged since the last tag.
example.outcome: It reads the history since that tag, checks what each change actually did and writes a dated entry grouped by type.

yeknal-agent-cost-control.title: Agent cost control
yeknal-agent-cost-control.purpose: Measures what agent work actually costs, finds the sessions and settings that own the spend, and changes one lever at a time without quietly losing review quality along the way.
whenToUse: The inference bill rose, or one task cost far more than expected.
You are choosing models or effort levels and want evidence rather than a hunch.
Someone asks whether prompt caching, model routing, or a cheaper tier will actually help.
yeknal-agent-cost-control.avoid: It does not decide who does the work and it does not review code. It will not present a saving without an outcome check that nothing important was dropped.

example.ask: Why did last month cost more than the month before, with the same workload?
example.outcome: It reads the harness usage log, shows that one long session carried most of the spend, checks whether caching is already warm, and recommends splitting the work at a boundary instead of switching models.

yeknal-animate.title: Web animation
yeknal-animate.purpose: Adds purposeful, accessible motion to components, pages, scrolling, gestures, SVG and canvas, with sensible timing and a reduced-motion fallback.
whenToUse: You are adding an entrance, transition or gesture to a web interface.
A component needs motion that explains a change instead of decorating it.
You want motion that stays smooth and respects reduced-motion settings.
yeknal-animate.avoid: To audit motion that already exists, use Review animations instead.

example.ask: Animate the settings drawer so it slides in from the right and can be interrupted halfway.
example.outcome: It picks the properties, duration and easing, builds an interruptible transition and adds a reduced-motion version.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog, drawing on Emil Kowalski’s design-engineering ideas as inspiration; no source was copied.

yeknal-animate-expo.title: Animation in Expo
yeknal-animate-expo.purpose: Builds animation for React Native and Expo apps with Reanimated, Gesture Handler, Expo Router and haptics, making the decisions that decide whether motion feels right on a device.
whenToUse: You are adding gestures, sheets, screen transitions or press feedback to an Expo app.
Motion stutters on a real device and you need it on the right thread.
You want haptics that match what the interface is doing.
yeknal-animate-expo.avoid: For animation on the web, use Web animation.

example.ask: Make the bottom sheet follow my finger and settle with a spring when I let go.
example.outcome: It wires the drag with Gesture Handler, runs the motion on the UI thread with Reanimated and hands off velocity to a spring.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog, drawing on Emil Kowalski’s design-engineering ideas as inspiration; no source was copied.

yeknal-apple-design.title: Apple-style interface design
yeknal-apple-design.purpose: Brings Apple’s approach to fluid, physical motion and interface design to the web, from springs and interruptible gestures to materials, depth and typography.
whenToUse: You are building drag, swipe or sheet interactions that should feel physical.
You want spring animation and momentum that can be interrupted.
Typography, translucency and depth need the restraint Apple interfaces are known for.

example.ask: Review our swipe-to-dismiss card and make it feel more like iOS.
example.outcome: It checks how the gesture tracks the finger, tunes the spring and velocity hand-off and adds a reduced-motion alternative.

yeknal-application-security.title: Application security
yeknal-application-security.purpose: Designs or hardens security across web apps, APIs, cloud setup, CI/CD pipelines and AI features, covering the OWASP-style risks a product is likely to face.
whenToUse: You are building authentication, authorization or an API that handles user data.
A project needs a broad security pass before launch.
You want secure defaults for headers, secrets, rate limits and logging.

example.ask: Harden the API before we launch: auth, rate limiting, headers and how secrets are handled.
example.outcome: It reviews each area against concrete risks, fixes what it can and lists anything that needs a decision from you.

yeknal-brandkit.title: Brand kit images
yeknal-brandkit.purpose: Generates polished brand-guideline boards, logo systems and identity presentations as images, with deliberate composition and sparse typography.
whenToUse: You want visual concepts for a new brand or product identity.
You need a brand-guidelines board to share with a team.
You are exploring logo directions before committing to one.
yeknal-brandkit.requirements: Needs an image-generation tool available to your agent.

example.ask: Create a brand board for a calm budgeting app: logo ideas, palette and type.
example.outcome: It plans the identity, then generates a board with logo concepts, colours, type and a couple of mockups.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Leonxlnx’s taste-skill collection.

yeknal-break-ui.title: Break UI
yeknal-break-ui.purpose: Stress-tests a screen with realistic worst-case data, such as long names, missing fields, huge counts and non-Latin text, and reports every break with its fix.
whenToUse: A screen looks fine with demo data and you want to know where it fails.
You are about to ship a list, table or card that shows user-supplied text.
You want a dev-only toggle between demo and worst-case states.

example.ask: Try the worst case on the team members table.
example.outcome: It fills the table with extreme but realistic data, shows the broken states and fixes overflow, wrapping and empty values.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Emil Kowalski’s skills collection.

yeknal-content-seo.title: Content and SEO
yeknal-content-seo.purpose: Guides useful content and search visibility together, from keyword patterns and page briefs to metadata, structured data, sitemaps, local search, earned links and AI citations.
whenToUse: You are choosing which queries to target and which pages should exist.
You are planning or rewriting pages and want them to be found.
Metadata, canonical tags, crawlability or structured data need an audit.
A local business is invisible in the map pack, or links and coverage need a plan.
Traffic moved and you need to separate a ranking loss from a click-through loss.
You want a site to be readable by search engines and AI search alike.

example.ask: Choose the queries worth targeting and tell me whether to update an existing page or create a new one.
example.outcome: It reads the live results, checks existing query and page data, and returns a decision, a brief and the evidence behind it.

yeknal-design-reference-research.title: Design reference research
yeknal-design-reference-research.purpose: Researches comparable products and collects references into an evidence ledger and brief, so design decisions come from what works rather than what’s fashionable.
whenToUse: You are about to design or redesign something and want evidence first.
The team disagrees about direction and needs references to compare.
You want patterns from real products, not gallery trends.

example.ask: Research how five scheduling apps handle rescheduling before we redesign ours.
example.outcome: It studies each flow, records what it saw and what it couldn’t verify, and writes a short brief with recommendations.

yeknal-design-taste-frontend.title: Design taste for the web
yeknal-design-taste-frontend.purpose: Designs and builds expressive landing pages, portfolios and marketing sites from real product evidence instead of reusable AI layouts.
whenToUse: A new web experience needs distinctive art direction and working code.
You want a landing page that doesn’t look like a template.
The brand has a story the layout should carry.
yeknal-design-taste-frontend.avoid: For an existing product, use Redesign an existing product instead.

example.ask: Design and build a launch page for our note-taking app that feels like ours.
example.outcome: It pulls the visual direction from the product itself, then builds a responsive page with real copy and states.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Leonxlnx’s taste-skill collection.

yeknal-domain-modeling.title: Domain modeling
yeknal-domain-modeling.purpose: Clarifies a project’s domain terms and boundaries and records the decisions in a glossary or architecture decision record.
whenToUse: People use different words for the same thing, or one word for two things.
System boundaries are unclear before a larger change.
You want a GLOSSARY.md or an ADR written down.

example.ask: We keep mixing up accounts, workspaces and organisations. Sort out the terms.
example.outcome: It maps how each term is used in code and conversation, proposes definitions and records them in a glossary.

attribution.credit: Written independently, inspired by the domain-modeling skill in Matt Pocock’s skills collection; no source text was copied.

yeknal-finalize.title: Finalize
yeknal-finalize.purpose: Runs the final documentation and quality checks, summarises the diff and handles any Git publishing you asked for.
whenToUse: The work is done and needs a last check before delivery.
You want a clear summary of what changed.
You are ready to commit and push but want the gates run first.

example.ask: Finalize this branch: run the checks, update the docs and push it.
example.outcome: It runs the repository’s checks, updates documentation that the change affects, summarises the diff and pushes.

yeknal-find-animation-opportunities.title: Find animation opportunities
yeknal-find-animation-opportunities.purpose: Looks through a codebase or interface for places that should animate and rejects those that shouldn’t, proposing motion with exact values but changing nothing.
whenToUse: You wonder what could be animated in an app.
An interface feels static and you want it to feel more alive.
You want proposals before anyone writes animation code.
yeknal-find-animation-opportunities.avoid: To fix existing animation, use Improve animations or Review animations.

example.ask: What in the onboarding flow would benefit from motion?
example.outcome: It lists a few specific opportunities with durations and easing, and explains why other spots should stay still.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog, drawing on Emil Kowalski’s design-engineering ideas as inspiration; no source was copied.

yeknal-frontend-design.title: Frontend design
yeknal-frontend-design.purpose: Sets a distinctive visual direction for new or heavily reshaped UI, from typography and composition to palette and interface copy.
whenToUse: You are designing a new screen or product surface.
A design looks generic and needs a clear point of view.
Typography, colour and layout need to work as one system.

example.ask: Design the pricing page so it doesn’t look like every other SaaS template.
example.outcome: It sets a visual direction from the product’s content, picks type and colour roles and builds the page with real copy.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Anthropic’s frontend-design skill. Its library guidance credits Rare UI, which requires attribution if you install one of its components.

yeknal-frontend-developer.title: Frontend developer
yeknal-frontend-developer.purpose: Implements or repairs accessible web interfaces in React, Vue or Angular, covering components, state, styling and browser behaviour.
whenToUse: You are changing frontend components or their state.
A browser behaviour or styling bug needs fixing.
You want accessible, working UI rather than a visual concept.

example.ask: Fix the date picker so it works with the keyboard and screen readers.
example.outcome: It repairs focus handling and labels, tests the keyboard path and keeps the existing look.

yeknal-gh-address-comments.title: Address PR comments
yeknal-gh-address-comments.purpose: Works through the review and issue comments on the open GitHub pull request for your current branch, using the GitHub CLI.
whenToUse: A pull request has review comments waiting.
You want each comment addressed or answered in turn.
You use the gh CLI and want the agent to read the PR directly.
yeknal-gh-address-comments.requirements: Needs the GitHub CLI signed in to your account.

example.ask: Address the review comments on my PR.
example.outcome: It checks gh is signed in, reads each comment, makes the changes and summarises what it did for each one.

attribution.credit: Adapted from GitHub’s published skill.

yeknal-gh-fix-ci.title: Fix failing CI
yeknal-gh-fix-ci.purpose: Inspects failing GitHub Actions checks on a pull request, summarises the logs, drafts a fix plan and only makes changes once you approve.
whenToUse: Checks are failing on a pull request.
You want the failure explained before anything changes.
CI runs on GitHub Actions.
yeknal-gh-fix-ci.avoid: Checks from other providers, such as Buildkite, are reported by link only.
yeknal-gh-fix-ci.requirements: Needs the GitHub CLI signed in to your account.

example.ask: The tests job is failing on my PR. Find out why.
example.outcome: It pulls the failing job’s logs, explains the cause, proposes a fix and waits for your go-ahead.

attribution.credit: Adapted from GitHub’s published skill.

yeknal-git.title: Git
yeknal-git.purpose: Handles status, diffs, branches, commits, merges and pushes while leaving unrelated work in your checkout alone.
whenToUse: You want a focused commit without sweeping in other changes.
You need help with a branch, merge or history question.
Your working tree has unrelated edits that must survive.

example.ask: Commit only the API changes and push them to a new branch.
example.outcome: It stages just those files, writes a clear commit message, creates the branch and pushes it.

yeknal-high-end-visual-design.title: High-end visual design
yeknal-high-end-visual-design.purpose: Creates art-directed, showcase-level web interfaces with a product-specific visual idea, expressive type, deliberate composition and considered motion.
whenToUse: The brief explicitly asks for agency, editorial or experimental quality.
A launch or showcase page needs a strong visual idea.
Ordinary product styling isn’t enough for this piece.
yeknal-high-end-visual-design.avoid: For everyday product UI, use Frontend design instead.

example.ask: Art-direct the launch page for our camera app as if it were a magazine feature.
example.outcome: It develops a visual thesis from the product, then builds a page with editorial type, imagery and restrained motion.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Leonxlnx’s taste-skill collection.

yeknal-human-ai-interface-design.title: Human-AI interface design
yeknal-human-ai-interface-design.purpose: Designs AI features people can trust, covering suggestions, generation, copilots and agents, along with sources, uncertainty, approvals and recovery.
whenToUse: You are adding an AI feature to a product.
Users need to see where an answer came from or how sure it is.
An agent can take actions that need approval or undo.

example.ask: Design how our assistant proposes calendar changes before it makes them.
example.outcome: It designs a review step with clear sources, editable proposals, approval and a way to undo.

yeknal-implement.title: Implement
yeknal-implement.purpose: Takes a scoped feature or fix from plan to working code while keeping the rest of the repository behaving as it did.
whenToUse: You want a feature built or a bug fixed from start to finish.
The change has to fit existing conventions and not break other behaviour.
You want the work verified rather than just written.

example.ask: Add CSV export to the reports page.
example.outcome: It reads how the page works today, adds the export following existing patterns and runs the flow to confirm it works.

yeknal-improve-animations.title: Improve animations
yeknal-improve-animations.purpose: Surveys an app’s existing motion like a senior motion designer would, then writes a prioritised audit with self-contained plans that other agents can carry out.
whenToUse: You want a roadmap of animation fixes across an app.
Motion feels inconsistent and you don’t know where to start.
You plan to hand the fixes to other agents or a cheaper model.
yeknal-improve-animations.avoid: It plans changes but doesn’t edit source code.

example.ask: Audit the motion across the dashboard and plan what to fix first.
example.outcome: It inventories each animation, ranks the problems and writes a standalone fix plan for each.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog, drawing on Emil Kowalski’s design-engineering ideas as inspiration; no source was copied.

yeknal-industrial-brutalist-ui.title: Industrial brutalist UI
yeknal-industrial-brutalist-ui.purpose: Designs raw, mechanical interfaces that mix Swiss print typography with terminal aesthetics: rigid grids, extreme type contrast and utilitarian colour.
whenToUse: You want a dashboard or site to feel like a declassified blueprint.
A data-heavy interface suits a stark, technical style.
The brief names brutalist or industrial aesthetics.

example.ask: Restyle the telemetry dashboard in an industrial brutalist style.
example.outcome: It sets a strict grid and type scale, a utilitarian palette and dense but readable data panels.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Leonxlnx’s taste-skill collection.

yeknal-launch-readiness.title: Launch readiness
yeknal-launch-readiness.purpose: Audits a product before it becomes publicly reachable, covering the legal obligations that attach to the data, payments, email and user content it handles, plus the engineering gates no other workflow owns, then returns one register and a go or no-go.
whenToUse: You are about to let strangers reach the product for the first time.
You need to know which privacy, payment, email and content duties apply to you, in Nigeria or elsewhere.
You want the unglamorous checks done: database rules, a tested restore, a real performance budget, deliverability, spend caps, a rollback plan.
yeknal-launch-readiness.avoid: It is not legal advice and it is not a code review. It never states a statutory maximum as a likely outcome, and it marks anything it cannot verify as unassessed rather than guessing.

example.ask: We launch on Monday. What are we missing?
example.outcome: It builds a data map from the code, checks it against the applicable obligations and the seven launch gates, then returns a verdict with blockers first, the filings that need lead time, and every check it could not perform.

yeknal-legacy-sweep.title: Legacy sweep
yeknal-legacy-sweep.purpose: Audits a whole repository or subsystem for unused legacy code and bloated or worthless tests, proves each candidate is obsolete before deleting it, fixes real defects instead of removing the failing test, and keeps the coverage that still protects behaviour.
whenToUse: A codebase has accumulated dead paths, unused exports and stale tests.
A test suite is slow or noisy and you want to prune it without losing the checks that matter.
A cleanup should fix the failures it uncovers instead of deleting them.
You want a cleanup that reports what it could not prove.
yeknal-legacy-sweep.avoid: It is not a lint pass and not a licence to delete code. Every removal needs a filled evidence row, a failing test is treated as a defect before it is treated as bloat, and it never authors unit tests.

example.ask: Sweep the repo: remove the dead code and the bloated tests, but fix real bugs instead of hiding them.
example.outcome: It records a baseline, splits production ownership into read-only and write lanes, removes only candidates with completed proof, fixes the failures that are real defects, and reports what it removed, the contracts it preserved and every blocked candidate.

attribution.credit: The test evidence gate was written independently, inspired by the test-audit concepts in the openclaw project; no source text was copied. Production-code, failure-triage and campaign material is original.

yeknal-markdown-management.title: Markdown management
yeknal-markdown-management.purpose: Creates, merges, updates and audits Markdown without losing meaning, links or repository conventions, including README files and Agent Skills.
whenToUse: Docs need merging or restructuring without losing anything.
A README or skill file needs updating to match the code.
You want links and headings audited.

example.ask: Merge these two setup guides into one README section.
example.outcome: It combines them without dropping steps, keeps the links working and follows the repository’s style.

yeknal-minimalist-ui.title: Minimalist UI
yeknal-minimalist-ui.purpose: Designs clean editorial interfaces with warm monochrome palettes, strong typographic contrast, flat grids and restrained depth.
whenToUse: The brief calls for calm, premium minimalism.
An interface feels cluttered and needs restraint.
You want typography to carry the hierarchy.

example.ask: Redesign the settings page in a warm, minimal editorial style.
example.outcome: It reduces the palette, strengthens the type hierarchy and groups settings with space instead of boxes.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Leonxlnx’s taste-skill collection.

yeknal-mobile-app-design.title: Mobile app design
yeknal-mobile-app-design.purpose: Designs and builds mobile screens and flows that feel native, especially in Expo or React Native, covering navigation, controls, states, accessibility and performance.
whenToUse: You are building screens for an Expo or React Native app.
Navigation or controls don’t feel like they belong on the platform.
Loading, empty and error states are missing on mobile.

example.ask: Design and build the checkout flow for our Expo app.
example.outcome: It plans the screens and navigation, builds them with native-feeling controls and covers each state.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Appllama’s skills collection.

yeknal-oil-motion.title: Frame-based motion
yeknal-oil-motion.purpose: Designs and builds scrubbable web animation made from generated or captured frames and driven by scroll, pointer, touch or data, for moments ordinary CSS can’t express.
whenToUse: A product transformation or scene change can’t be done with CSS alone.
You want an animation that follows the scroll or the pointer frame by frame.
Media needs processing into an efficient, scrubbable sequence.
yeknal-oil-motion.avoid: For ordinary UI transitions, use Web animation.
yeknal-oil-motion.requirements: Frame processing may need Python 3, Pillow and ffmpeg.

example.ask: Make the product photo rotate as the visitor scrolls through the feature section.
example.outcome: It plans the frames, processes them into an efficient sequence and wires playback to the scroll position.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Lin Zhihuang’s oil-motion skill.

yeknal-orchestration-specialists.title: Orchestration specialists
yeknal-orchestration-specialists.purpose: Organises work across several agents and tools, covering task distribution, context management, evidence synthesis, prompt engineering and MCP design.
whenToUse: A job is big enough to split between agents.
Context is getting lost between steps.
You are designing prompts or an MCP server.

example.ask: Split this migration across agents so each one handles a service and reports back.
example.outcome: It divides the work into bounded tasks, defines what each agent returns and merges the results with evidence.

yeknal-performance.title: App performance
yeknal-performance.purpose: Measures startup, screen navigation, content loading and scrolling on a throttled production build, finds the real bottleneck, then proves each fix with before and after benchmarks rather than intuition.
whenToUse: The app feels slow to start or slow to open a screen.
Content takes too long to appear, especially older or deeper pages.
Scrolling stutters or degrades during a long session.
Every optimization needs a measured before and after.
yeknal-performance.avoid: It is not failure diagnosis or a motion audit. Use Troubleshoot for a broken feature and Improve animations for motion craft.

example.ask: Make this app faster, benchmark every fix, and tell me what actually worked.
example.outcome: It records a cold production baseline on a throttled device, traces the largest cost, changes one thing at a time, re-measures, and keeps only the wins that clear the noise floor.

yeknal-pick-ui-library.title: Pick a UI library
yeknal-pick-ui-library.purpose: Recommends the right library or inspectable source registry for a frontend need from a curated list, from accessible primitives to charts, toasts and drag and drop.
whenToUse: You need a component library and don’t want to guess.
You are choosing between options for charts, menus or virtualised lists.
You want something accessible and actively maintained.
yeknal-pick-ui-library.avoid: It only runs when you ask for it by name.

example.ask: Which library should I use for an accessible command menu in React?
example.outcome: It compares a few candidates from its list and recommends one with reasons and install notes.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog. It mentions Rare UI, which requires attribution if you install one of its components.

yeknal-playwright.title: Browser automation
yeknal-playwright.purpose: Lets your agent open a real browser from the terminal to click through a flow, fill forms, take screenshots and read what’s on the page, so it can show you a change working.
whenToUse: You want proof that a sign-up, checkout or settings flow still works after a change.
A layout problem only shows up at one screen size or after a few clicks.
You need screenshots or page text captured the same way every time.
yeknal-playwright.avoid: If you want a permanent test suite in the repository, ask for Playwright test files instead, because this skill drives the browser from the command line.
yeknal-playwright.requirements: Needs Node.js with npx, which the bundled wrapper uses to run playwright-cli.

example.ask: Open the sign-up page at phone width, fill the form with test values and send me a screenshot of the confirmation screen.
example.outcome: It opens a browser through the bundled wrapper, steps through the form, saves the screenshot and reports anything that overlapped or clipped.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Microsoft’s playwright-cli skill, including its NOTICE.txt attribution.

yeknal-project-handoff.title: Project handoff
yeknal-project-handoff.purpose: Keeps a short HANDOFF.md at the root of the repository so the next session, or the next person, can pick up exactly where the work stopped.
whenToUse: A project spans several sessions or people.
You are finishing a milestone and want the context saved.
You are picking up an unfamiliar repository.

example.ask: Update the handoff with where we got to today.
example.outcome: It records the current state, decisions, how to verify the work and what remains, without repeating what the code already shows.

yeknal-prototype.title: Prototype variants
yeknal-prototype.purpose: Builds several genuinely different versions of a UI piece behind a visual picker, so you can flip between them live and keep the one that feels right.
whenToUse: You can’t decide between layouts until you see them working.
You want to compare real, interactive options rather than mockups.
A component needs exploring before it’s finalised.
yeknal-prototype.avoid: It only runs when you ask for it by name.

example.ask: Prototype three different empty states for the inbox.
example.outcome: It builds three distinct versions with a picker to switch between them, ready for you to promote one.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog, drawing on Emil Kowalski’s design-engineering ideas as inspiration; no source was copied.

yeknal-redesign-existing-projects.title: Redesign an existing product
yeknal-redesign-existing-projects.purpose: Refreshes the look or flow of a working site or app without breaking its behaviour or the data behind it.
whenToUse: A product works but looks dated or generic.
Responsive layouts are broken and need repairing.
You want UX improvements without rewriting the app.

example.ask: Give the admin dashboard a visual refresh without changing how anything works.
example.outcome: It inventories every route and state first, then restyles them while keeping each feature behaving the same.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Leonxlnx’s taste-skill collection. Its library guidance credits Rare UI, which requires attribution if you install one of its components.

yeknal-research-analysis.title: Research and analysis
yeknal-research-analysis.purpose: Researches and compares sources, checks them against each other and writes evidence-backed reports for market, competitive, trend or data questions.
whenToUse: You need a report backed by sources rather than opinion.
You are comparing competitors or tools.
A question needs deep research across many sources.

example.ask: Compare the main open-source feature-flag tools for a small team.
example.outcome: It gathers current sources, compares the tools on the criteria that matter and cites where each claim came from.

attribution.credit: Includes material adapted from NeetigyaShah’s deep-research skill.

yeknal-review.title: Code review
yeknal-review.purpose: Reads code or a whole system for real defects, regressions and maintainability risks, then sorts what it finds by severity and effort.
whenToUse: You want a second opinion before merging.
A system needs a quality assessment.
You want findings you can act on, not style nitpicks.

example.ask: Review the payments module for bugs and risky code.
example.outcome: It reports concrete defects with locations and reasons, ranked by severity, and suggests fixes.

yeknal-review-animations.title: Review animations
yeknal-review-animations.purpose: Checks existing motion against a high craft bar, from easing and duration to interruption and reduced-motion behaviour, and explains each fix.
whenToUse: You are reviewing a change that adds or alters animation.
Motion feels slow, floaty or janky.
You want specific fixes rather than general advice.

example.ask: Review the animations in this pull request.
example.outcome: It checks each animation’s purpose, timing and easing, and suggests concrete changes with values.

attribution.credit: Written for this catalog, drawing on Emil Kowalski’s design-engineering ideas as inspiration; no source was copied.

yeknal-security-audit.title: Security audit
yeknal-security-audit.purpose: Runs a multi-phase security audit of a repository, directory or diff with a coverage ledger, adversarial verification and schema-validated findings.
whenToUse: You want a full security audit or pen test of a codebase rather than a quick review.
You need findings you can hand to someone else, with evidence and a reproduction for each.
A previous audit needs its coverage gaps closed or its findings rechecked against changed code.
yeknal-security-audit.avoid: It only runs a full audit when you ask for one. Security questions and focused reviews belong to the narrower security skills.
yeknal-security-audit.requirements: Needs Node.js for the two zero-dependency validators. Target code is not executed without an OS-enforced sandbox.

example.ask: Audit this repository for security vulnerabilities and give me the findings.
example.outcome: It plans coverage, hunts in isolated units, has every candidate independently disproved or confirmed, and writes findings.json plus a report derived from it.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Cloudflare's security-audit skill.

yeknal-security-best-practices.title: Security best practices
yeknal-security-best-practices.purpose: Reviews Python, JavaScript, TypeScript or Go code for security issues and writes secure-by-default code when you ask for it.
whenToUse: You want a security review of specific code.
New code should be secure by default from the start.
You are working in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript or Go.
yeknal-security-best-practices.avoid: It only runs for explicit security review or secure-coding requests.

example.ask: Do a security review of the file-upload handler.
example.outcome: It checks validation, storage, paths and permissions, and reports issues with fixes and references.

attribution.credit: An original workflow that incorporates OpenAI’s security review material.

yeknal-security-ownership-map.title: Security ownership map
yeknal-security-ownership-map.purpose: Maps who owns sensitive code from Git history and highlights bus-factor risk and code nobody looks after.
whenToUse: You want to know who maintains authentication or payment code.
Sensitive areas may depend on one person.
You are writing or checking a CODEOWNERS file.
yeknal-security-ownership-map.avoid: It only runs when you ask about security ownership.

example.ask: Who owns our auth and billing code, and where are we exposed?
example.outcome: It analyses commit history for sensitive paths and reports owners, gaps and single points of failure.

attribution.credit: An original workflow that incorporates OpenAI’s security review material.

yeknal-security-threat-model.title: Threat model
yeknal-security-threat-model.purpose: Builds a threat model grounded in the actual repository, covering assets, trust boundaries, abuse paths and mitigations.
whenToUse: You are launching something that handles sensitive data.
You want to understand how the system could be abused.
A security review needs a threat model first.
yeknal-security-threat-model.avoid: It only runs when you ask for a threat model.

example.ask: Threat model the new public API.
example.outcome: It maps assets and trust boundaries from the code, lists likely abuse paths and recommends mitigations by priority.

attribution.credit: An original workflow that incorporates OpenAI’s security review material.

yeknal-sentry.title: Sentry errors
yeknal-sentry.purpose: Inspects Sentry issues and events, summarises recent production errors and pulls basic health data, using read-only queries.
whenToUse: You want a summary of recent production errors.
A specific Sentry issue needs investigating.
You want health numbers without opening the dashboard.
yeknal-sentry.requirements: Uses Python and needs a SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN.

example.ask: What are the top errors in production this week?
example.outcome: It queries Sentry read-only and summarises the most frequent issues with links and affected users.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Sentry’s published skill.

yeknal-slopscan.title: Slop scan
yeknal-slopscan.purpose: Scans a codebase locally for AI-slop indicators such as stock marketing copy, placeholder text, gradient headline text, decorative emoji, stock icon sets and kit default colors, and writes a report that explains each finding and how to fix it.
whenToUse: You want to know whether a codebase carries the familiar signs of a shipped template.
Copy or interface patterns need checking before a launch.
You want findings with locations and fixes rather than a general opinion.
yeknal-slopscan.avoid: It reads source files only. It cannot see the rendered page, so checks that need a browser are reported as unassessed.

example.ask: Scan this project for AI slop before we launch.
example.outcome: It reports each indicator with its file and line, a plain explanation and a fix, lists what it could not assess, and writes both a readable log and a JSON report.

yeknal-testing-strategy.title: Testing strategy
yeknal-testing-strategy.purpose: Keeps verification end to end: proves behavior through the real entry point, bans new unit tests, and asks before any isolated check.
whenToUse: You are about to add tests for a feature.
You want coverage of real user flows and error paths.
An agent is about to write unit tests instead of an end-to-end flow.

example.ask: Plan how we should test the new password-reset flow.
example.outcome: It maps the flow's real end-to-end path and failure states, then proposes the browser or CLI run that proves them and leaves a rerunnable record.

yeknal-troubleshoot.title: Troubleshoot
yeknal-troubleshoot.purpose: Works back from a reproducible error, failing build or slowdown to its cause before it suggests a fix.
whenToUse: Something broke and you don’t know why.
A build or deployment fails with an unclear error.
Performance got worse after a change.

example.ask: The app crashes when I open the settings page. Figure out why.
example.outcome: It reproduces the crash, traces it to the cause, fixes it and confirms the page opens.

yeknal-ui-quality-baseline.title: UI quality baseline
yeknal-ui-quality-baseline.purpose: Applies a shared set of visual, responsive, accessibility, state, motion and copy checks whenever an agent creates or changes visible UI.
whenToUse: You want every UI change held to the same standard.
Layouts break at small widths or with large text.
Loading, empty and error states keep getting forgotten.

example.ask: Check the new onboarding screens against the UI baseline.
example.outcome: It checks spacing, contrast, focus, responsive containment and states, then fixes what fails.

yeknal-ui-ux-designer.title: UI and UX design
yeknal-ui-ux-designer.purpose: Designs user-centred interface systems that balance intuitive flows with a distinctive visual direction, from information architecture to interaction patterns.
whenToUse: You are shaping how a product is organised and navigated.
A flow is confusing and needs rethinking.
You need a UI specification someone can build from.

example.ask: Rethink how people find and manage saved reports.
example.outcome: It maps the current flow, proposes a clearer structure and specifies the screens and interactions.

yeknal-verification-harness.title: Verification harness
yeknal-verification-harness.purpose: Generates a project-local skill that launches the real app, drives a feature the way a user would, and captures proof, with a feature map for the next agent to follow.
whenToUse: A repository has no scripted way to prove its UI, CLI or service behavior.
You are tired of re-deriving how to start the app and check a flow.
You want screenshots, transcripts or response bodies kept as evidence.
yeknal-verification-harness.avoid: It builds the harness; for what counts as proof, use Testing strategy.

example.ask: This repo has no way to prove a flow end to end. Set one up.
example.outcome: It inspects how the app starts and can be driven, writes a verify skill with launch, doctor, drive, evidence and cleanup, seeds a feature map and then proves it once.

attribution.credit: Adapted from Lauren Tan's pstack skill of the same name.

yeknal-yeet.title: Commit, push and open a PR
yeknal-yeet.purpose: Stages, commits, pushes and opens a GitHub pull request in one flow using the GitHub CLI.
whenToUse: You want the whole commit-to-PR flow done in one go.
Your changes are ready and reviewed locally.
You use the gh CLI.
yeknal-yeet.avoid: It only runs when you explicitly ask for the full flow.
yeknal-yeet.requirements: Needs the GitHub CLI signed in to your account.

example.ask: Yeet this: commit, push and open a PR.
example.outcome: It stages the changes, writes the commit, pushes the branch and opens a pull request with a summary.

attribution.credit: Adapted from OpenAI’s published skills.

yeknal-deploy.title: Deploy
yeknal-deploy.purpose: Detects the hosting provider from repository configuration and follows that provider's deploy procedure, so an unnamed "deploy this" request has one entry point instead of four competing ones.
whenToUse: The user asks to deploy, host, publish or push a site live.
The provider is unstated and has to be read from wrangler, netlify, render or vercel configuration.
A deploy failed and the provider-specific recovery step is needed.
yeknal-deploy.avoid: It is not a hosting comparison and not an infrastructure provisioner. It detects a provider, runs the documented path, and stops to ask when two configurations match.

example.ask: Deploy this app and give me the live link.
example.outcome: It reads the repository configuration, identifies the provider, follows that provider's preview-first procedure, and reports the deployed URL and any missing credentials.

attribution.credit: Provider procedures are adapted from the four previously separate deploy skills, whose licence files moved with the content into references/licenses.
